claim: Planarian flatworms regenerate every organ after amputation.
source: Planarian flatworms regenerate every organ after amputation.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that establishes the regenerative capacity of planarians.

claim: Adult pluripotent stem cells drive planarian regeneration ability.
source: Adult pluripotent stem cells drive this ability, but how injury activates and directs stem cells into the appropriate lineages is unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field of planarian biology.

claim: Brief exposure of planarians to sodium azide selectively induces ejection of the pharynx.
source: Here we describe a single-organ regeneration assay in which ejection of the planarian pharynx is selectively induced by brief exposure of animals to sodium azide.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: An RNAi screen of 356 genes upregulated after amputation was performed using successful feeding as a proxy for regeneration.
source: To identify genes required for pharynx regeneration, we performed an RNAi screen of 356 genes upregulated after amputation, using successful feeding as a proxy for regeneration.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Knockdown of 20 genes caused a wide range of regeneration phenotypes.
source: We found that knockdown of 20 genes caused a wide range of regeneration phenotypes and that RNAi of the forkhead transcription factor FoxA, which is expressed in a subpopulation of stem cells, specifically inhibited regrowth of the pharynx.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RNAi screen described in the manuscript.

claim: FoxA is expressed in a subpopulation of stem cells.
source: We found that knockdown of 20 genes caused a wide range of regeneration phenotypes and that RNAi of the forkhead transcription factor FoxA, which is expressed in a subpopulation of stem cells, specifically inhibited regrowth of the pharynx.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FoxA expression patterns in stem cells.

claim: RNAi of FoxA specifically inhibited regrowth of the pharynx.
source: We found that knockdown of 20 genes caused a wide range of regeneration phenotypes and that RNAi of the forkhead transcription factor FoxA, which is expressed in a subpopulation of stem cells, specifically inhibited regrowth of the pharynx.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments.

claim: The hematopoietic system can replenish the entire blood in an animal from a single stem cell after bone marrow transplants.
source: For example, the hematopoietic system can replenish the entire blood in an animal from a single stem cell after bone marrow transplants (Lagasse et al., 2001; Shizuru et al., 2005), and hair follicle and epidermis can regenerate in mammals following injury (Fuchs and Segre, 2000; Seifert et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Hair follicle and epidermis can regenerate in mammals following injury.
source: For example, the hematopoietic system can replenish the entire blood in an animal from a single stem cell after bone marrow transplants (Lagasse et al., 2001; Shizuru et al., 2005), and hair follicle and epidermis can regenerate in mammals following injury (Fuchs and Segre, 2000; Seifert et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: After amputation, even small planarian fragments can support regrowth of entire animals.
source: After amputation, even small fragments can support regrowth of entire animals (Morgan, 1898; Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004), indicating that the resident cells have the capacity to self-renew, and can replace all of the missing tissues comprising the animal (including muscle, nervous system, digestive system, excretory system and epithelial cells).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Planarian regenerative capacity depends on a population of stem cells termed neoblasts.
source: This regenerative capacity depends on a population of stem cells termed neoblasts (Reddien and Sánchez Alvarado, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Neoblasts are pluripotent cells that are constantly dividing.
source: These pluripotent cells are constantly dividing, driving replenishment of all cell types during homeostasis (Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2000; Pellettieri and Sánchez Alvarado, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Upon amputation, neoblasts are stimulated to divide rapidly.
source: Upon amputation, neoblasts are stimulated to divide rapidly (Baguñà, 1976; Reddien et al., 2005a; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010) and begin to differentiate, but how these stem cells are regulated to produce only the tissues that need to be replaced is unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neoblasts exhibit heterogeneity across the population in terms of both gene expression and cell cycle status.
source: One hypothesis for how stem cells can produce any tissue in the planarian body on demand is that these cells exhibit heterogeneity across the population, in terms of both gene expression and cell cycle status (Rink, 2012; Reddien, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Heterogeneity has been observed molecularly by gene expression-profiling of neoblasts purified via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS).
source: Heterogeneity has been observed molecularly by gene expression-profiling of neoblasts purified via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) (Hayashi et al., 2010; Shibata et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Some, but not all, stem cells can repopulate and rescue animals lacking stem cells in single-cell transplantation experiments.
source: Functional evidence of such heterogeneity is supported by single-cell transplantation experiments in which some, but not all, stem cells can repopulate and rescue animals lacking stem cells (Wagner et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Discrete subpopulations of neoblasts express markers of differentiated tissues.
source: Recent studies have also demonstrated that discrete subpopulations of neoblasts express markers of differentiated tissues (Scimone et al., 2011; Lapan and Reddien, 2012; Cowles et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The planarian pharynx is a complex organ consisting of multiple tissues including neurons, muscle, epithelial cells and secretory cells.
source: The planarian pharynx serves as both the entrance and exit to the digestive system and is a complex organ consisting of multiple tissues including neurons, muscle, epithelial cells and secretory cells (Hyman, 1951; Ishii, 1962; MacRae, 1963; Kido, 1964).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The pharynx clearly lacks dividing stem cells.
source: The pharynx is a large cylindrical structure that clearly lacks dividing stem cells (Hay and Coward, 1975; Newmark and Sánchez Alvarado, 2000; Orii et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mesenchymal cells adopt pharyngeal fate prior to accumulation in the nascent pharynx during de novo pharynx regeneration.
source: Previous experiments describing de novo pharynx regeneration in head and tail pieces have shown that mesenchymal cells adopt pharyngeal fate prior to accumulation in the nascent pharynx (Asai, 1991; Bueno et al., 1997; Cebrià et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Soaking animals in sodium azide for a brief period of time caused the pharynx to be extruded and then dislodged completely from the rest of the animal following gentle agitation.
source: We found that soaking animals in sodium azide for a brief period of time caused the pharynx to be extruded, and then dislodged completely from the rest of the animal following gentle agitation (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data and images in Figure 1.

claim: Within several days the pharynx regenerated after chemical amputation.
source: Within several days the pharynx regenerated, as visualized either in live animals or by hybridization with a pharynx-specific riboprobe (Figure 1C; Cebrià et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and images in Figure 1C.

claim: Other organs, including the gastrointestinal system, were unaffected at a gross morphological level after sodium azide treatment.
source: Other organs, including the gastrointestinal system, were unaffected at a gross morphological level (Figure 1D), indicating that sodium azide treatment causes selective amputation of the pharynx without noticeably perturbing other organs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and images in Figure 1D.

claim: Within 24 hr of amputation, small, undifferentiated cells accumulate at the entry to the intestine, within the mesenchyme.
source: Within 24 hr of amputation, small, undifferentiated cells accumulate at the entry to the intestine, within the mesenchyme (Figure 1E, white arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Two days after amputation, cells begin to organize, characterized by a layer of ciliated epithelial cells, a concentration of neurons, and a subepidermal muscle layer.
source: Two days after amputation, these cells begin to organize, characterized by a layer of ciliated epithelial cells, a concentration of neurons, and a subepidermal muscle layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three days after amputation the lumenal connection to the intestine has been restored.
source: Three days after amputation the lumenal connection to the intestine has been restored, radial symmetry has been re-established, and most genes expressed in the mature pharynx are present, including the secreted Frizzled-related protein sFRP-1, ciliary dynein heavy chain DNAH-β3, and two members of the Nou Darake family of FGF-receptor-like proteins ndk and ndl-3 (Rink et al., 2011; 2009; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: 100% of animals regenerated pharynges after chemical amputation (n > 1000).
source: Even though the regeneration of chemically amputated pharynges appears to proceed normally by all histological and molecular measures, and 100% of animals regenerated pharynges after amputation (n > 1000), we wished to further test whether the brief exposure to sodium azide during chemical amputation might cause secondary effects in regeneration, particularly soon after the treatment.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments.

claim: Transverse amputations performed in sodium azide showed that wound healing occurred normally after washout.
source: To test the possibility that sodium azide broadly compromised regenerative potential, we performed transverse amputations in sodium azide. After washout, wound healing occurred normally, indicating that animals recovered rapidly from sodium azide treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The mitotic profile triggered by amputation during the early phase of regeneration was indistinguishable from controls in fragments amputated in sodium azide.
source: Furthermore, in these regenerating fragments, the mitotic profile triggered by amputation during the early phase of regeneration was indistinguishable from controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure of animals to lethal doses of gamma-irradiation completely prevents stem cell division and regeneration.
source: Exposure of animals to lethal doses of gamma-irradiation completely prevents stem cell division and regeneration (Bardeen and Baetjer, 1904).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Lethal irradiation (10,000 rads γ-irradiation) completely prevented pharynx regeneration in 100% of animals (n = 100 animals).
source: Radiation completely prevented pharynx regeneration (Figure 2A) in 100% of animals (n = 100 animals) indicating that, as expected, stem cells are required for regeneration.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from irradiation experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Lethal irradiation inhibited the accumulation of cells at the wound site 24 hr after amputation.
source: Furthermore, lethal irradiation inhibited the accumulation of cells at the wound site 24 hr after amputation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the first cells to arrive at the wound site are either neoblasts or their descendants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Smedwi-2 phenocopies radiation by inhibiting stem cell function.
source: Similarly, RNAi knockdown of the planarian piwi/Argonaute protein Smedwi-2 phenocopies radiation by inhibiting stem cell function (Reddien et al., 2005b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Smedwi-2(RNAi) animals failed to regenerate the pharynx (0/33 animals, compared to 24/24 control animals).
source: Indeed, Smedwi-2(RNAi) animals failed to regenerate the pharynx (0/33 animals, compared to 24/24 control animals) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pharynx regeneration depends on functional neoblasts.
source: These results indicate that pharynx regeneration, like all other regeneration in planaria, depends on functional neoblasts and that large reserves of post-mitotic cells competent to become pharyngeal tissues are unlikely to exist.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the irradiation and RNAi experiments.

claim: In planaria, amputation stimulates two characteristic waves of proliferation: within hours of any wound, mitotic events increase throughout the body, and 2 days later proliferation is localized to the wound.
source: In planaria, amputation stimulates two characteristic waves of proliferation: within hours of any wound, mitotic events increase throughout the body, and 2 days later proliferation is localized to the wound (Baguñà, 1976; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In the first 24 hr after chemical amputation, there was a sharp but transient decrease in overall mitotic activity.
source: In the first 24 hr after amputation, we observed a sharp but transient decrease in overall mitotic activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), presumably due to the metabolic suppression effects of sodium azide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant enrichment of mitotic nuclei around the pharynx wound site 24 hr after amputation.
source: Indeed, we found a significant enrichment of mitotic nuclei around the pharynx wound site, indicating that the proliferative response induced by pharynx removal generates a sufficiently powerful signal to induce and maintain proliferation where regeneration is necessary.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of mitotic activity shown in Figure 2E.

claim: During the first 24 hr after amputation, 718 genes were enriched upon pharynx removal (log2 fold change>0.4, adjusted p<0.05).
source: Because we aimed to identify transcripts that were essential for the initiation of pharynx regeneration, we first focused on genes upregulated during the first 24 hr after amputation. During this window, 718 genes were enriched upon pharynx removal (log2 fold change>0.4, adjusted p<0.05) and we cloned 274 of these genes.
evidence: This is a result from the microarray expression profiling experiment.

claim: 21/42 genes examined showed distinct upregulation in the area around the regenerating pharynx by whole-mount in situ hybridization.
source: To validate our microarray data, we examined the expression patterns of several upregulated genes during pharynx regeneration with whole-mount in situ hybridization. We found that 21/42 of these genes showed distinct upregulation in the area around the regenerating pharynx, as expected (Supplementary file 1B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from validation experiments.

claim: Animals regained the ability to eat 7 days after chemical amputation.
source: Animals regained the ability to eat 7 days after amputation (Figure 3B), indicating that all of the tissues comprising the pharynx were present, functional, and integrated with the rest of the animal by this point in regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The RNAi screen identified 20 genes (5.6% of total) that caused reproducible defects in feeding behavior upon knockdown.
source: Using feeding behavior as a proxy for pharynx regeneration, we screened the 356 cloned genes by RNA-interference. We considered a 50% defect in food uptake as our initial threshold and identified 20 genes (5.6% of total) that caused reproducible defects in this assay upon knockdown (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNAi screen.

claim: After three doses of FoxA(RNAi), 35/50 animals developed a lesion on their dorsal side through which they subsequently ejected their pharynx.
source: In our screen, after three doses of FoxA(RNAi), animals developed a lesion on their dorsal side through which they subsequently ejected their pharynx (Figure 4A, 35/50 animals).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FoxA RNAi experiments.

claim: Three days after amputation, control animals had regenerated the arrayed muscle fibers covered by epithelial cells, along with the ciliated cells that extend to the distal tip of the pharynx.
source: Three days after amputation, control animals had regenerated the arrayed muscle fibers covered by epithelial cells, along with the ciliated cells that extend to the distal tip of the pharynx (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FoxA(RNAi) pharynges appeared as a disorganized mass of cells, lacking obvious muscle fibers and any epithelial covering.
source: By contrast, FoxA(RNAi) pharynges appeared as a disorganized mass of cells, lacking obvious muscle fibers and any epithelial covering (Figure 4C), indicating both a failure to produce the cells comprising the pharynx and to pattern them properly.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FoxA(RNAi) tail pieces successfully regenerated nervous system tissue that was indistinguishable from controls, but failed to form a new pharynx.
source: FoxA(RNAi) tail pieces successfully regenerated nervous system tissue that was indistinguishable from controls, but failed to form a new pharynx (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FoxA(RNAi) head fragments had no defect in intestinal growth or patterning.
source: FoxA(RNAi) head fragments had no defect in intestinal growth or patterning (Figure 4E), demonstrating that FoxA controls regeneration of the pharynx but not other organs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FoxA controls regeneration of the pharynx but not other organs.
source: FoxA(RNAi) head fragments had no defect in intestinal growth or patterning (Figure 4E), demonstrating that FoxA controls regeneration of the pharynx but not other organs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on head and tail regeneration.

claim: The anterior marker Sfrp1 and the posterior marker nou darake-like-3 (ndl-3) were re-established properly 7 days after amputation in FoxA knockdown animals.
source: The anterior marker Sfrp1 and the posterior marker nou darake-like-3 (ndl-3) were re-established properly 7 days after amputation in FoxA knockdown animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that FoxA is not required for specifying expression of these markers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of Wnt11-5 in FoxA(RNAi) tail fragments does not reset the anterior boundary at the pharynx as sharply and reproducibly as controls.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Wnt11-5 in FoxA(RNAi) tail fragments does not reset the anterior boundary at the pharynx as sharply and reproducibly as controls (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: In adult planarians, FoxA is expressed strongly in the mature pharynx and in scattered cells in the mesenchyme surrounding the pharynx.
source: In adult planarians, FoxA is expressed strongly in the mature pharynx (Koinuma et al., 2000; Umesono et al., 2013), and in scattered cells in the mesenchyme surrounding the pharynx (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations.

claim: After pharynx amputation, FoxA+ cells accumulated both in the nascent pharynx and tissue surrounding the pharyngeal pouch, adjacent to the wound site.
source: We observed that after pharynx amputation, FoxA+ cells accumulated both in the nascent pharynx and tissue surrounding the pharyngeal pouch, adjacent to the wound site (Figure 5B, top row).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Radiation exposure completely inhibited accumulation of FoxA+ cells and caused a depletion of the mesenchymal cells surrounding the pharynx.
source: Radiation completely inhibited accumulation of FoxA+ cells and caused a depletion of the mesenchymal cells surrounding the pharynx (Figure 5B, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In intact animals, a subset of smedwi-1 cells also expressed FoxA in the vicinity of the pharynx.
source: We performed double fluorescent in situ hybridization with FoxA and smedwi-1. Although FoxA is expressed relatively weakly compared to smedwi-1, in intact animals we found a subset of smedwi-1 cells that also expressed FoxA in the vicinity of the pharynx (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Following pharynx removal, the percentage of FoxA+smedwi-1+ cells increased significantly, with the peak occurring 3 days after pharynx removal.
source: Indeed, following pharynx removal, the percentage of FoxA+smedwi-1+ cells increased significantly, with the peak occurring 3 days after pharynx removal (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 3 days after amputation, FoxA was strongly expressed in the epithelial cells and only weakly in the muscle cells and neurons.
source: 3 days after amputation, when the pharynx has regenerated its cylindrical structure with regularly arrayed muscle fibers and concentrated neurons at its distal tip (Figure 4B), FoxA was strongly expressed in the epithelial cells and only weakly in the muscle cells and neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: As regeneration proceeded, FoxA expression in the epithelial cells diminished and became more pronounced throughout the interior part of the pharynx.
source: Interestingly, as regeneration proceeded, FoxA expression in the epithelial cells diminished and became more pronounced throughout the interior part of the pharynx (Figure 6B), which is enriched for muscle and neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The overall distribution of stem cells was comparable in FoxA(RNAi) and control animals.
source: Examination of the pattern of Smedwi-1+ neoblasts showed that the overall distribution of stem cells was comparable in FoxA(RNAi) and control animals (Figure 6C), demonstrating that the neoblasts were not detectably affected by knockdown of FoxA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Body-wide and local proliferation during regeneration was indistinguishable from controls in FoxA(RNAi) animals.
source: Consistent with this observation, body-wide and local proliferation during regeneration was indistinguishable from controls (Figure 6D,E) indicating that FoxA is not required for stimulation of proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Approximately 3 weeks after initiating RNAi, a pronounced dorsal outgrowth formed over the pharynx in 70% of FoxA(RNAi) animals (n > 100).
source: Interestingly, approximately 3 weeks after initiating RNAi, a pronounced dorsal outgrowth formed over the pharynx in 70% of animals (n > 100).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from long-term RNAi experiments.

claim: The dorsal outgrowths in FoxA(RNAi) animals lacked any recognizable anatomical features of control pharynges, such as radial symmetry or clear laminar structure.
source: Histological analysis of FoxA(RNAi) animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) demonstrated that this dorsal outgrowth lacked any recognizable anatomical features of control pharynges, such as radial symmetry or clear laminar structure.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dorsal outgrowths in FoxA(RNAi) animals failed to express either of two pharynx-specific markers (Smed-laminin and Smed-npp-1) or the intestine-specific marker Smed-porcupine.
source: Consistent with this observation, these dorsal outgrowths also failed to express either of two pharynx-specific markers (Smed-laminin and Smed-npp-1) (Collins et al., 2010) or the intestine-specific marker Smed-porcupine (Figure 6F), indicating that this aberrantly produced tissue does not acquire pharyngeal or endodermal fate.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Enrichment of neuronal markers (Smed-PC2 and Smed-ndk) and the muscle marker Smed-collagen was identified in the dorsal outgrowths of FoxA(RNAi) animals.
source: However, we did identify enrichment of neuronal markers (Smed-PC2 and Smed-ndk) and the muscle marker Smed-collagen, which suggests that in the absence of FoxA, differentiation into neurons and muscle remains intact.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: FoxA expression remained strongly suppressed 20 days after the final administration of RNAi.
source: To eliminate the possibility that this dorsal outgrowth is an incomplete pharynx formed by restoration of FoxA levels after the dsRNA inhibition has weakened, we examined FoxA expression 20 days after the final administration of RNAi, and found that it remained strongly suppressed (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: FoxA likely acts to restrict differentiation of new tissues into the pharynx lineage.
source: Because these types of abnormal outgrowths were never observed in chemically amputated animals or in any other RNAi contexts, we conclude that FoxA likely acts to restrict differentiation of new tissues into the pharynx lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Knockdown of genes functioning upstream of FoxA would inhibit accumulation of FoxA+ progenitors, while genes functioning downstream of FoxA would not affect FoxA distribution.
source: We took advantage of this feature of FoxA to establish a molecular pathway for genes identified in our screen, reasoning that knockdown of genes functioning upstream of FoxA would inhibit accumulation of FoxA+ progenitors, while genes functioning downstream of FoxA would not affect FoxA distribution.
evidence: This is the reasoning behind the epistasis analysis.

claim: Failure to accumulate FoxA+ cells was observed in irradiated animals and in Smedwi-2(RNAi) animals.
source: Indeed, failure to accumulate FoxA+ cells was observed in irradiated animals (Figure 5B) and in Smedwi-2(RNAi) animals (Figure 7A), confirming that inhibiting stem cell function alters accumulation of FoxA+ progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B and 7A.

claim: Knockdown of MCM7, ribonucleotide reductase, RuvB, cyclin D1, SAE-2, CPSF-3, and zmym-1 caused complete inhibition of FoxA progenitor accumulation.
source: As expected, knockdown of these genes caused complete inhibition of FoxA progenitor accumulation, as well as a failure to maintain the mesenchymal population of FoxA+ cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PABP-2(RNAi) caused a severe decrease in the number of FoxA+ precursors accumulating in or around the pharynx.
source: For example, PABP-2(RNAi) caused a severe decrease in the number of FoxA+ precursors accumulating in or around the pharynx (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Knockdown of WDR3 and WDR36 caused an unusual distribution of FoxA+ precursors, with streams and clumps of FoxA+ cells present in the mesenchyme but directed toward the nascent pharynx.
source: Knockdown of WDR3 and WDR36 caused an unusual distribution of FoxA+ precursors (Figure 7B, white arrows), with streams and clumps of FoxA+ cells present in the mesenchyme but directed toward the nascent pharynx.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ribonucleotide reductase, cyclin D1, and RuvB accumulated strongly around the nascent pharynx in FoxA(RNAi) animals.
source: Interestingly, ribonucleotide reductase, cyclin D1, and RuvB accumulated strongly around the nascent pharynx in FoxA(RNAi) animals (Figure 7C, white arrows), providing further evidence that in the absence of FoxA, stem cells are prevented from differentiating into the pharyngeal lineage.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Chemical amputation produces wounds of exactly the same size, which normalizes both the extent of mitotic activity and the degree of apoptosis.
source: Second, chemical amputation produces wounds of exactly the same size, which normalizes both the extent of mitotic activity and the degree of apoptosis, both known to correspond directly with wound size (Pellettieri et al., 2010; Wenemoser and Reddien, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FoxA functions as a pioneer transcription factor, opening chromatin due to its structural similarity to linker histones and activating transcription of endoderm-specific genes.
source: FoxA functions as a pioneer transcription factor, opening chromatin due to its structural similarity to linker histones and activating transcription of endoderm-specific genes (Cirillo et al., 2002; Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Eeckhoute et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: This study represents the first indication that FoxA functions in regeneration.
source: Although it has been previously characterized in development and cancer (Lupien et al., 2008), our study represents the first indication that FoxA functions in regeneration.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: FoxA is known to define organ identity during development.
source: FoxA is known to define organ identity during development (Gaudet and Mango, 2002) and to directly modify chromatin structure (Cirillo et al., 2002), leading to a hypothesis that during planarian regeneration, FoxA plays an analogous role.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FoxA is not required for regenerating or patterning organs besides the pharynx.
source: Because FoxA(RNAi) animals still established expression of anterior/posterior patterning molecules and regenerated head and tail structures normally, we conclude that FoxA is not required for regenerating or patterning organs besides the pharynx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: FoxA mRNA was expressed in multiple tissue types as regeneration progressed.
source: FoxA mRNA was expressed in multiple tissue types as regeneration progressed, suggesting that FoxA activation in stem cells is the first step toward differentiation of several pharynx-specific cell types.
evidence: This is supported by double FISH data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: FoxA transcript is present in the stem cell population, like other transcription factors that are critical for brain, photoreceptor, and excretory system development in planaria.
source: Our data demonstrate that FoxA transcript is present in the stem cell population, like other transcription factors that are critical for brain, photoreceptor, and excretory system development in planaria (Lapan and Reddien, 2011; Scimone et al., 2011; Cowles et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research and data from this study.

claim: The stem cell population alters its output in response to complete organ amputation.
source: However, in the case of pharynx regeneration, we can monitor the percentage of FoxA+ stem cells in response to complete organ amputation, demonstrating that the stem cell population alters its output in response to organ amputation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In C. elegans, the DNA helicase RuvB functions in a genetic pathway with FoxA to regulate pharynx organogenesis.
source: Interestingly, in C. elegans, the DNA helicase RuvB functions in a genetic pathway with FoxA to regulate pharynx organogenesis (Updike and Mango, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In planaria, RuvB is required for stem cell function.
source: Our results demonstrate that in planaria, RuvB is required for stem cell function, but it may also play a role in properly specifying progenitors during regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the RNAi screen.

claim: Induction of supernumerary pharynges or engraftment of transplanted pharynges only occurs at a distance from the resident pharynx.
source: In planarians, induction of supernumerary pharynges or engraftment of transplanted pharynges only occurs at a distance from the resident pharynx, suggesting that an inhibitory activity is present in the peripharyngeal region (Ziller-Sengel, 1967a, 1967b; Schilt, 1972).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published research.
